extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and scholars (those studying patent claim scope and patentable subject-matter)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what subject-matter is patentable (principles, properties, processes, machines) and how claims/specifications should be construed — with illustrative case law (Foote v. Silsby, Le Roy v. Tatham, Neilson, Morse, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for an art or principle in the abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that undertakes to cover an art or principle in the abstract (e.g., 'the cutting of ice of a uniform size by means of an apparatus worked by any other power than human') renders the patent void, unless a timely disclaimer saves it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim attempts to appropriate an abstract principle or art rather than a concrete application or apparatus, courts will treat it as non-patentable. Example: a broad first clause claiming an art generally was likely 'mere surplusage' and not the invention; the patent properly covered only the apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apparatus claims from abstract statements; surplusage may be disregarded
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim includes both a general (possibly abstract) clause and a specific clause, the invention may reside in the specific clause and the general clause be treated as surplusage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will look to the face of the claim to find where the invention resides; non-misleading surplus language need not invalidate the patent but may be rejected as inessential. Draft claims to focus on the concrete machine/method that embodies the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a natural property by mechanical contrivances can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of a natural property or principle (e.g., expansive/contractive power of a metallic rod by heat) to a practical purpose, effected by mechanical contrivances, may constitute patentable subject-matter if the patentee was the first to make that application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under decisions like Foote v. Silsby (as interpreted by Justice Nelson), the new application of a principle by mechanical means can be 'of itself a part of his invention,' and different or improved modes of application may still be treated as improvements that fall within the patentee's rights (subject to competing doctrines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposite doctrine — appropriation limited to the particular means used (plus equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrary view holds that appropriation cannot extend to the abstract application of a principle; it extends only to the application as effected by the particular means used by the patentee, and to mechanical equivalents, colorable imitations, or fraudulent evasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this narrower approach, a patentee's monopoly is limited to the specific combination or modes disclosed (and their equivalents), and genuine improvements in the means are not automatically captured. Determination often hinges on whether accused device is a mechanical equivalent or a real improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of a general claim depends on novelty of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: A general claim that purports to cover the application of a principle (independent of the particular device) is valid only if the patentee was the first to make that application; novelty of the general application is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trials may try issues of novelty for both the general application and particular combinations. Even if a jury finds against a general claim, courts in equity may uphold a patent on particular combination claims where novelty of the combination exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery + practical application of a new property of matter is patentable if sufficiently enabled
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical application of a newly discovered property of matter (e.g., a property of lead) is a patentable invention if the specification describes a process sufficiently to enable an ordinary mechanic to construct and apply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Le Roy v. Tatham and related authorities show that novelty may rest in the new property and its application rather than novel machinery. But if the specification does not sufficiently describe the process (or the claim is drafted to claim something else), the patent may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: If machinery is old, the invention may still be the new application of the machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the combination of machinery employed is old, its new application to develop or employ a newly discovered property (producing effects new in kind) can constitute an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will assess whether the new use produces effects 'new in kind' (e.g., a new and useful product or manufacture). If the new result depends on the discovered property and its embodiment, a patent may be sustained despite old apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and claim construction should be liberal and substance-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification and claim should be construed 'benignly' — looking through inartificial phrases to the substance of what was really invented, to protect the patentee's true discovery when ascertainable from the specification as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will take the specification and patent together, avoid hyper-technical invalidation on forms of expression, and try to identify the 'thing really invented' if the language fairly supports it. Drafting should still be clear, but courts may interpret imperfect language liberally to effect the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter: principle must be embodied to a practical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere abstract principle is not patentable; but a principle 'so far embodied and connected with corporeal substances as to be in a condition to act, and to produce effects' for a practical object may be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chief Justice Eyre's doctrine: if the principle is turned to account for a practical object (a mode of carrying the principle into effect), it is patentable. Draft claims to show embodiment/operation to avoid being characterized as an abstract principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: New product/substance vs mechanism/process distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the effect produced is a new substance or composition, the exclusive right may be to making that new substance regardless of mechanism; if not a new substance, the patentable subject-matter is the mechanism (if new) or the new process/method of operating (even with old mechanism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction (from Eyre) guides claim strategy: seek product claims when invention yields a new article; otherwise claim the novel mechanism or novel process of operation producing the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency: describe process sufficiently for an ordinary mechanic
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent grounded on the application of a new property must describe the devices or process sufficiently to enable an ordinary mechanic to construct and apply the necessary process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification fails to teach how to practice the invention, the patent may be invalid even if a new principle is described. Emphasize clear, enabling disclosure in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/purposive claim limitations tie scope to use and may preserve validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that limits a combination to its use for a specified purpose or 'in any other manner substantially the same' (e.g., 'when used to form pipes of metal, under heat and pressure, in the manner set forth, or in any other manner substantially the same') ties the claim to the employment of the new property and may avoid a claim to the machinery per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use purposive functional limitations to show that the claimed combination is claimed only in the context of the novel application; this can prevent construction that the patentee claimed the apparatus in the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of protection against other modes once inventor provides a mode of carrying principle into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person discovers a principle or property and invents some mode of carrying it into effect, he is entitled to protection against all other modes which carry the same principle into practice for obtaining the same effect or result; infringement analysis then focuses on substantial identity of principle and application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Forsyth, Jupe, Neilson) recognize that protection may extend beyond the precise contrivances described if the accused mode is merely another way of carrying the same principle into effect. The inquiry centers on whether the accused means effect the same application/principle (mechanical means matter only insofar as they affect identity).
